elements.quote: Vaccination against severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection plays a key role in the containment of the coronavirus disease (COVID19) pandemic. All vaccines approved by the European Medical Agency (EMA) at the time of writing demonstrated high vaccine efficacy/effectiveness (VE) against severe COVID-19. With vaccination programmes being implemented in most European countries, it becomes urgent to assess the extent to which these vaccines are also able to prevent symptomatic and asymptomatic infections to guide public health recommendations and develop strategies for fully vaccinated people.
elements.reason: Provides the current state (EMA-approved vaccines show high efficacy vs severe COVID-19) and identifies an important uncertainty/knowledge gap (extent to which vaccines prevent symptomatic and asymptomatic infections) motivating the review.

elements.quote: Evidence on COVID-19 vaccine efficacy/effectiveness (VE) in preventing asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infections is needed to guide public health recommendations for vaccinated people. We report interim results of a living systematic review.
elements.reason: Explicitly states the importance and need for the review to guide public health recommendations and reports interim results of a living systematic review addressing that need.

No evidence provided that discusses existing similar systematic reviews or explains the specific need for this review compared to prior reviews; no citations of prior reviews or statements about updating/replicating previous reviews were found in the supplied evidence.

elements.quote: VE against infection can also be regarded as an indicator of how well a vaccine prevents transmission. In addition, studies suggest that persons who become SARS-CoV-2-positive despite vaccination had a shorter duration of virus shedding and lower viral load [8].
elements.reason: Provides partial mechanistic information (reduced viral load and shorter shedding as explanations for reduced transmission) but does not explicitly describe the vaccine's mechanism of action (e.g., immune response pathways); therefore only partial.

The review concerns vaccine efficacy/effectiveness; there is no indication in the supplied evidence that the intervention is a complex, multi-component delivery context requiring a logic model, so this conditional item does not apply.

elements.quote: In detail, we report the interim results of the review focusing on two research questions: What is the efficacy/effectiveness of COVID-19 vaccines in preventing SARS-CoV-2 infections (irrespective
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states that the review focuses on two research questions and begins to state a specific question about vaccine efficacy/effectiveness in preventing SARS-CoV-2 infection, indicating explicit objectives/questions.

elements.quote: see Supplement Part S2 for complete population intervention comparison outcomes (PICO) questions
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly refers to PICO questions and points to Supplement Part S2 for the complete population-intervention-comparison-outcomes, indicating that planned comparisons are stated using a PICO framework.

elements.quote: We considered studies of any design as long as they had a comparison group that investigated VE against SARS-CoV-2 infection and/or asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection after vaccination with an EMA-approved COVID-19 vaccine (see Supplement Part S2 for complete population intervention comparison outcomes (PICO) questions).
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies key eligibility components (population, intervention, outcomes, requirement for a comparison group, restriction to EMA-approved vaccines) and refers to a PICO in the supplement; it does not explicitly list all study characteristics (e.g. settings, specific follow-up requirements) within the provided evidence.

elements.quote: No restrictions were made regarding publication language or status. The review started on 1 January 2021. The end date of this interim analysis was 14 May 2021.
elements.reason: The report explicitly states language and publication-status eligibility (no restrictions) and gives the review start and end dates, addressing dissemination timing.
No explicit distinction is provided in the retrieved evidence between excluding studies because outcomes were not measured versus excluding because outcome results were not reported.

elements.quote: | Study population (n)                           | General population (cases: n = 35,979; controls: n = 35,979) | HCW (n = 9,109) | ... | Study design                                   | Case-control study (test-negative design) | Retrospective cohort study | ... | Vaccine                                        | Comirnaty | Comirnaty | ...
elements.reason: The manuscript and tables present and distinguish groups used in analyses (e.g. vaccinated vs unvaccinated, vaccine types, dose 1 vs dose 2, populations such as HCW or LTCF), but there is no clear, explicit statement linking each synthesis grouping to the specific comparisons defined in the review objectives in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: We considered studies of any design as long as they had a comparison group that investigated VE against SARS-CoV-2 infection and/or asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection after vaccination with an EMA-approved COVID-19 vaccine ... With vaccination programmes being implemented in most European countries, it becomes urgent to assess the extent to which these vaccines are also able to prevent symptomatic and asymptomatic infections to guide public health recommendations and develop strategies for fully vaccinated people.
elements.reason: The report restricts eligibility to EMA-approved vaccines and provides a rationale (focus on EMA-approved vaccines because of their relevance for public health recommendations and the need to assess their effectiveness).

No study registers, regulatory databases, or online repositories with associated names and date restrictions are reported in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: These interim results of a living systematic review show that after completed course the EMA-approved COVID-19 vaccines have a VE of 80% to 90% in preventing SARS-CoV2 infections, including asymptomatic ones. We found some indication that VE estimates are not reduced in cases infected with variant of concern (VOC) Alpha (Phylogenetic Assignment of Named Global Outbreak (Pango) lineage designation B.1.1.7), however these results should be interpreted with caution. VE against infection can also be regarded as an indicator of how well a vaccine prevents transmission. In addition, studies suggest that persons who become SARS-CoV-2-positive despite vaccination had a shorter duration of virus shedding and lower viral load [8]. ... At the time point of data cut for this interim analysis, only limited information was available on VOCs other than Alpha. Meanwhile, some studies have been published indicating reduced effectiveness against infections with VOC Delta for Comirnaty and Vaxzevria, whereas effectiveness against hospitalisation was unchanged, as compared to VOC Alpha [34,35].
elements.reason: The discussion explicitly interprets the review results (VE 80–90%) and compares them to other evidence: noting findings for VOC Alpha, citing studies about viral shedding/viral load, and mentioning more recent studies showing reduced effectiveness against Delta—thereby placing results in context of other evidence.

elements.quote: Some of our methodological limitations stem from the rapidly changing publication landscape of COVID-19 vaccine studies. In particular, non-randomised studies on real-world effectiveness are continuously and frequently published on preprint servers. Although we systematically searched seven preprint servers, additional studies could have been published on other servers or websites that we did not capture. Moreover, it has to be considered that these studies did not undergo peer review and should therefore be considered with caution. A recent study reported that some final journal publications of COVID-19 studies differ to a certain extent from versions which were previously published on pre-print servers [33]. A further limitation is the small number of countries where the studies were performed, including the possibility that some studies, in particular those from Israel and the US, might have analysed partly overlapping study populations. The majority of studies included were conducted in persons vaccinated with Comirnaty. At the time point of data cut for this interim analysis, only limited information was available on VOCs other than Alpha.
elements.reason: The Discussion explicitly states multiple limitations of the included evidence: rapidly changing publication landscape, reliance on preprints (not peer reviewed), possible missing studies, potential overlapping populations, limited geographic diversity, dominance of one vaccine in included studies, and limited data on variants — thereby discussing limitations of the evidence.
